standard_text: Understand the concept of a unit rate and use terms related to rate in the context of a ratio relationship.

progression.narrative: 6.RP.2 turns the ratio idea into the rate idea: two quantities traveling together, anchored to a second quantity of exactly 1. The logic runs from recognizing to making to using to defending. First a student must know a unit rate when they see one (S1) — the defining feature is the 1, often hiding inside 'per' or 'each.' Then they MAKE unit rates: scale a given ratio down to 'something to 1' by dividing both parts (S2), and pull the same move off the standard's two sanctioned models — a rate table and a double number line — where the unit rate may live between the printed ticks and may even be a decimal the model never shows (S3). With the unit rate in hand, the standard reverses direction: multiply it back up to test which scaled statements are true (S4), and run the full round trip in a real context — divide a rate down to 1, then use it to solve, with the unit phrase ('minutes per lap') dictating the division's direction (S5). Finally, students step up to the standard's DOK 3 demand: critique flawed rate work, where the classic bug is a flipped setup with flawless arithmetic, and a real critique names the error, explains it, and provides the fix (S6).

steps.rationale: 'Understand the concept of a unit rate' starts with recognition: a unit rate is a rate whose second quantity is exactly 1, and words like 'per' and 'each' hide that 1. Every later step tests against this definition.
Move from spotting to making: any ratio scales down to a unit rate by dividing both parts by the second quantity. The rate table makes the target visible — the unit rate is whatever pairs with 1.

The spec limits models to tape diagrams and double number lines, and its hardest items hide the unit rate between the printed ticks. Reading a model means asking it the per-1 question, not copying its first labeled pair.
'Use terms related to rate' runs forward too: a known unit rate predicts every scaled amount by multiplication. Judging true/false rate statements forces compute-then-compare instead of guessing.

The At-Proficiency demand is the full round trip in context: divide a real-world rate down to 1, with the unit phrase choosing the division's direction, then multiply the unit rate up to answer a new question.

The standard's Above-Proficiency band asks students to reason through, critique, and justify. The signature bug — a flipped rate with perfect arithmetic — can only be caught by auditing the setup against the question's units.

skills.name: Divide whole numbers fluently to find one group's share

prerequisite_skill.description: Recall basic division facts and divide a two-digit number by a one-digit number

skills.i_do_script: Every unit rate in this standard comes from one division: the total, divided by how many groups. Watch me do one: 42 stickers shared by 6 friends. I ask, '6 times WHAT gets me to 42?' 6 x 7 = 42, so each friend gets 7. We're going to get fast at that one move — total divided by groups — because it's the engine behind every rate problem this week.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides in the wrong direction or reaches for subtraction when a total must be split into equal groups
canonical_error.example: For '42 stickers shared by 6 friends,' student computes 42 - 6 = 36, or tries 6 / 42 and stalls
canonical_error.why: The student hasn't anchored division to the equal-groups picture — 'total split into groups' — so with two numbers on the page they fall back on the most familiar operation, or divide the small number by the big one because that's the order the numbers appeared.

skills.item_template: A short division prompt, either bare (54 / 9 = ?) or one-line equal-share context. No choices — student writes the quotient. Whole-number answers only, facts through 12s.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 36 signals subtraction; 48 signals addition; 252 signals multiplication
45 signals subtraction; a stall signals missing fact recall for 9s
64 signals subtraction; 8 signals dividing 8 by itself
32 signals subtraction; 8 signals a near-miss fact (4 x 8 = 32)
8 signals the 7 x 8 = 56 near-miss fact
7 signals the 6 x 7 = 42 near-miss fact
11 signals a near-miss; a stall signals facts stop at 10s
6 signals the 8 x 6 = 48 near-miss fact
40 signals subtraction; 8 signals a near-miss fact
11 signals a near-miss; a stall signals facts stop at 10s
55 signals subtraction; 11 signals a near-miss fact
8 signals the 9 x 8 = 72 near-miss fact

sample_items.stem: Share 40 pencils among 8 kids. Each gets ?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 32 signals subtraction; 48 signals addition

sample_items.stem: Split $66 across 6 people. Each gets $?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 60 signals subtraction; 10 signals a near-miss fact
110 signals subtraction; 11 signals a near-miss fact

redirect_script.stop: Hold on — what are we splitting?
redirect_script.prompt: Point to the total, then point to the number of groups. Say it as a sentence: 'the TOTAL divided by the GROUPS.' Now ask yourself: the groups number times WHAT gets me to the total?
redirect_script.praise: You split the total by the groups — that's exactly the move.

vocabulary.definition: The answer you get when you divide one number by another.
Groups that all have exactly the same amount in them.
The whole amount before it gets split up.

next_steps.if_fail: Drill division facts with a fact-family chart (6 x 7 = 42, so 42 / 6 = 7) before returning to this skill.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: '42 stickers are shared equally by 6 friends. How many stickers does each friend get?'
What is the total in this story, and what is it being split into?
When a total gets split into equal groups, that's division: total divided by groups. Here that's 42 divided by 6.
Instead of dividing cold, flip it into a multiplication question: 6 times WHAT equals 42?
If the student writes 42 - 6 or tries 6 / 42, don't correct it yet — ask them to draw 6 circles and deal out the 42. The picture forces the right operation.
So each friend gets 7. Check it backward: does 6 x 7 really rebuild the total of 42?
That backward check — groups times share equals total — is how you'll verify every rate answer in this standard.
Your turn, no picture this time: 54 stamps shared by 9 albums. Total divided by groups — go.

skills.name: Read and write a ratio in words, colon, and fraction form

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two quantities and keep track of which number describes which thing
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In 'a bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles,' which number goes with red?

skills.i_do_script: Draw the bowl before any numbers: 2 circles labeled 'apple' and 3 circles labeled 'orange.' Every ratio we write is just pointing at those two piles in a chosen order -- point at the wrong pile first and the numbers flip on you. A ratio is just a comparison of two amounts, and this standard writes it three ways that all mean the same thing: '2 to 3', 2:3, and 2/3. Watch me with a real one: a fruit bowl has 2 apples for every 3 oranges. I can say '2 to 3', write 2:3, or write the fraction 2/3 — apples on top because apples came first. The one rule that never bends: the order of the words is the order of the numbers.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the order of the two quantities when converting between forms
canonical_error.example: For 'the ratio of oranges to apples' with 2 apples and 3 oranges, student writes 2:3 instead of 3:2
canonical_error.why: The student matches numbers to the order they appeared in the story instead of the order in the question's phrase, because they don't yet treat 'A to B' as a fixed slot structure where the first word claims the first number.

skills.item_template: A one-sentence context with two labeled quantities. Student writes the ratio in a requested form (words, colon, or fraction), or picks the statement that matches a given ratio. MC or short response.

sample_items.stem: A team has 4 forwards and 5 guards. Write the ratio of forwards to guards using a colon.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5:4 signals the order swap; 9 signals adding the quantities

sample_items.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour and 2 cups of sugar. Write the ratio of sugar to flour using a colon.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3:2 signals matching story order instead of question order

sample_items.stem: Which fraction shows the ratio of 7 dogs to 4 cats?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4/7 is the order swap; 7/11 and 4/11 compare a part to the total instead of part to part

sample_items.stem: Write '9 wins to 2 losses' as a ratio with a colon.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2:9 signals the order swap; 11 signals adding

sample_items.stem: A class has 12 girls and 15 boys. Which statement matches the ratio 15:12?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'girls to boys' is the order swap; the other two compare to the total

sample_items.stem: Write the ratio 5:8 in words.
sample_items.distractor_logic: '8 to 5' signals the order swap; '5.8' signals reading the colon as a decimal point

sample_items.stem: A parking lot has 6 trucks and 10 cars. Write the ratio of trucks to cars as a fraction.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 10/6 signals the order swap; 6/16 signals part-to-total

sample_items.stem: Which ratio means the same as the fraction 3/7?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7:3 is the order swap; 3:10 and 7:10 mix in the total

sample_items.stem: A garden has 8 tulips and 3 roses. Write the ratio of roses to tulips using the word 'to'.
sample_items.distractor_logic: '8 to 3' signals matching story order instead of the order the question asks for

redirect_script.stop: Wait — check the order of the words.
redirect_script.prompt: Underline the phrase that names the ratio, like 'sugar to flour.' The FIRST word claims the FIRST number. Now label each number in your ratio with its word and see if the labels match the phrase.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the order of the words to the order of the numbers — that's the whole game.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two amounts, like 2 apples for every 3 oranges.
Writing a ratio with the : symbol, like 2:3.
Which quantity comes first in a ratio — 'A to B' always puts A's number first.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the two piles: 2 circles labeled 'apple,' 3 circles labeled 'orange.' Now say 'apples to oranges' out loud while pointing at the piles as you say each word. Which pile did your finger land on first -- so which number has to come first?
Write on the board: 'A fruit bowl has 2 apples and 3 oranges.' Below it write the three blank forms: ___ to ___,  ___:___,  ___/___.
If I ask for the ratio of apples to oranges, which word comes first — and so which number has to come first?
Right: '2 to 3.' All three forms say the same thing — 2 to 3, 2:3, and the fraction 2/3. Same comparison, three costumes.
Fill in all three forms: 2 to 3, 2:3, 2/3. Label each number with its fruit.
Now the trap: what is the ratio of ORANGES to apples? What changes?
If the student says 2:3 again, don't correct — point at the phrase and ask them to label each number with its word. The mismatch shows itself.
Why does 3:2 mean something different from 2:3, even though it's the same two numbers?
Your turn: a shelf has 5 comics and 4 novels. Write 'novels to comics' in all three forms.

skills.name: Identify a unit rate statement in a real-world context
skills.i_do_script: A rate compares two different kinds of amounts — miles and hours, dollars and pounds. A UNIT rate is the special one where the second amount is exactly 1: '30 miles per 1 hour,' '$3 for 1 pound.' Watch me sort two statements: '120 miles in 4 hours' is a rate, but not a unit rate — the hours aren't 1. '30 miles per hour' IS a unit rate, because 'per hour' secretly means 'per 1 hour.' The whole skill is hunting for the 1.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls any statement with two quantities a unit rate, without checking that the second quantity is exactly 1
canonical_error.example: Student picks 'Jade drove 120 miles in 4 hours' as the unit rate instead of 'Jade drove 30 miles per hour'
canonical_error.why: The student has attached 'unit rate' to 'comparison with numbers and units' but not to the defining feature — the second quantity must be 1. They also miss that words like 'per' and 'each' hide an invisible 1.

skills.item_template: Four real-world statements; exactly one compares a quantity to exactly 1 unit (often hidden inside 'per' or 'each'). Student selects the unit rate. MC with 4 choices.

sample_items.stem: Which statement describes a unit rate?
sample_items.answer: A car travels 45 miles per hour.
choices: A car travels 45 miles per hour.
A car travels 90 miles in 2 hours.
A car used 3 gallons of gas today.
A car took 2 hours to travel 45 miles.
sample_items.distractor_logic: '90 miles in 2 hours' is a rate but not per 1; '3 gallons today' is a single quantity, not a comparison; '2 hours to travel 45 miles' flips the comparison and still isn't per 1

sample_items.stem: Which statement describes a unit rate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '$40 for 5' is an equivalent rate but the second quantity isn't 1; '8 tickets' has no comparison; '5 students shared $8' compares but not to 1

sample_items.stem: Which statement describes a unit rate?
sample_items.answer: The printer prints 12 pages each minute.
choices: The printer prints 12 pages each minute.
The printer prints 60 pages in 5 minutes.
The printer printed 12 pages this morning.
The printer took 5 minutes to warm up.
sample_items.distractor_logic: '60 in 5 minutes' isn't per 1; the last two are single quantities with no comparison — 'each minute' is the hidden 1

sample_items.stem: Which statement describes a unit rate?
choices: A shopper bought 3 pounds of grapes.
A shopper spent $9 at the store.
sample_items.distractor_logic: '$9 for 3 pounds' is the same rate not scaled to 1; the other two are lone quantities, not comparisons

redirect_script.stop: Hold on — where's the 1 in that statement?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the second quantity in each statement — the one after 'in,' 'for,' or 'per.' A unit rate needs that number to be exactly 1. Remember 'per hour' and 'each minute' are hiding a 1. Which statement passes the test?
redirect_script.praise: You hunted for the 1 — that's exactly what makes a rate a UNIT rate.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio that compares two different kinds of units, like miles and hours.
A rate where the second amount is exactly 1, like 30 miles per 1 hour.
A word that means 'for each 1' — '$3 per pound' means $3 for every 1 pound.

worked_example_script.text: Write the question and its four choices on the board: 'Which statement describes a unit rate?  (a) A car travels 45 miles per hour.  (b) A car travels 90 miles in 2 hours.  (c) A car used 3 gallons of gas today.  (d) A car took 2 hours to travel 45 miles.' Tell students exactly one is a unit rate.
Start from the definition: a unit rate compares two different amounts, and the second amount is exactly 1. Our whole job is to hunt for the 1.
Look at (b), '90 miles in 2 hours.' What two amounts is it comparing, and what is the SECOND amount? Is that a 1?
So (b) is a rate — but not a UNIT rate, because 2 isn't 1. Now (a), '45 miles per hour.' The 1 is hiding — what does 'per hour' actually mean?
Rewrite (a) as '45 miles per 1 hour' and circle the 1. There's the second amount, exactly 1 — so (a) is the unit rate.

If a student picks (b) '90 miles in 2 hours' because 'it has miles AND hours,' don't correct — ask them to circle the second quantity in each choice and check whether it is exactly 1. The 2 in (b) fails the test; only (a) hides a 1.
Now the last two: (c) '3 gallons today' and (d) '2 hours to travel 45 miles.' Is (c) even a rate — what's missing? And in (d), is the second amount a 1?
Confirm it: which choice is the unit rate, and how did finding the hidden 1 prove it? (a — 45 miles per 1 hour.)

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: a unit rate compares an amount to exactly ___ of the other unit.
Rewrite '25 miles per hour' so the hidden 1 is visible.
practice_problems.answer: 25 miles per 1 hour

practice_problems.stem: Which is a unit rate: 'a faucet drips 10 times in 5 minutes' or 'a faucet drips 2 times per minute'? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: '2 times per minute' — 'per minute' means per 1 minute; the other compares to 5 minutes, not 1.
practice_problems.notes: Both are rates; only one is a UNIT rate. Listen for 'per 1.'

practice_problems.stem: Is '$18 for 6 notebooks' a unit rate? If not, what would the unit rate be?
practice_problems.answer: No — 6 is not 1. The unit rate is $3 per 1 notebook (18 / 6 = 3).
practice_problems.notes: Bridges toward S2: students who can reject it can start fixing it.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus picked the unit rate. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Choices: 'Ana biked 24 miles in 3 hours' and 'Ana biked 8 miles per hour'
Marcus chose: 'Ana biked 24 miles in 3 hours' -- 'it has both miles AND hours, so it's the unit rate.'
practice_problems.answer: Marcus checked for two units but never checked for the 1. A unit rate needs the second amount to be exactly 1 — 'Ana biked 8 miles per hour' means 8 miles per 1 hour, so it is the unit rate.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error: any two-quantity statement gets called a unit rate.

practice_problems.stem: Sort these: 'A' 3 cookies each day, 'B' 21 cookies in 7 days, 'C' 21 cookies total. Which is a unit rate, which is a rate, which is neither?
practice_problems.answer: A is a unit rate ('each day' = per 1 day); B is a rate but not a unit rate; C is neither — it compares nothing.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own unit rate statement about reading pages, and a second statement that is a rate but NOT a unit rate for the same situation.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'I read 6 pages per minute' (unit rate) and 'I read 30 pages in 5 minutes' (rate, not unit rate).
practice_problems.notes: Producing both shows ownership — the pair must describe the same speed.

practice_problems.stem: 'Ben scored 5 goals to 1 assist' has a 1 as its second number. Is it a unit rate the way '5 dollars per 1 pound' is? Discuss what makes it feel different.
practice_problems.answer: It fits the form — 5 goals per 1 assist — so it can be read as a unit rate; it feels different only because both units belong to the same game. The test is still the 1.
practice_problems.notes: Spec allows same or different units across the two quantities.

activities.title: Unit Rate or Not?
materials: 12 statement cards (below), three labeled header cards
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the three headers: Unit rate, Rate (not unit), Not a rate.
2. Partners sort all 12 cards, reading each aloud.
3. Rule: before a card lands in 'Unit rate,' the pair must point to the 1 (or the word hiding it — per, each, every).
4. Debrief: which card fooled you, and what word decided it?

activities.title: Say It Three Ways
activities.instructions:
1. Match each word statement to its colon form and its fraction form.
2. Both partners must agree the ORDER matches the words before claiming a triple.
3. Debrief: what does the 1 look like in each form?

activities.title: Hidden 1 Hunt
materials: A read-aloud list of rate statements
activities.instructions:
1. Read a statement aloud ('The car gets 32 miles per gallon').
2. Students write U on their board if it's a unit rate, R if it's a rate but not unit, N if it's not a rate — then boards up together.
3. One student must defend the majority answer by naming where the 1 is (or isn't).
4. Mix in traps: statements with a 1 as the FIRST number ('1 pizza feeds 4 people' — that IS a unit rate read the other way; discuss!) and lone quantities.

strategy_links.why: Deciding whether a statement is a unit rate is a fast, defensible claim — perfect for pair up, justify, and vote.
The definition ('a unit rate compares to exactly 1') is a crisp choral line that builds the automatic per-1 check.
U/R/N whiteboard responses instantly show who is calling every two-number statement a unit rate.

questioning_prompts: Where is the 1 in that statement — written down, or hiding inside a word?
What two kinds of amounts are being compared? Now, is the second one exactly 1?
What word in the statement means 'for each 1'?
Is that a rate at all? What TWO things would it have to compare?
Could you turn that rate into a unit rate? What would you have to do to the numbers?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks any statement with two quantities and units as 'the unit rate,' like '120 miles in 4 hours.'
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the second quantity in each statement — the one after 'in,' 'for,' or 'per.' A unit rate needs that number to be exactly 1. Remember 'per hour' and 'each minute' are hiding a 1. Which statement passes the test?
misconception_redirects.praise: You hunted for the 1 — that's exactly what makes a rate a UNIT rate.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student rejects '15 miles per hour' as a unit rate because 'there's no 1 anywhere.'
misconception_redirects.say: Read 'per hour' slowly — per means 'for each 1.' Rewrite the statement with the 1 showing and then decide.
misconception_redirects.praise: You translated 'per' into 'for each 1' — now the hidden 1 can't sneak past you.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs up or down: is '$28 for 4 shirts' a unit rate?
quick_checks.look_for: Thumbs down with 'the 4 isn't a 1.' A thumbs up means the student is still equating 'has two quantities' with 'unit rate.'

quick_checks.prompt: Say a unit rate about your own walk to class.
quick_checks.look_for: Any statement with a per-1 structure ('about 2 hallways per minute'). A lone quantity ('it takes 5 minutes') signals the comparison idea hasn't landed.

sentence_starters: It is a unit rate because the second amount is ___.
The word ___ is hiding the 1 in this statement.

worked_solution.stem: Which statement describes a unit rate? (a) 'A train travels 240 miles in 3 hours.' (b) 'A train travels 80 miles per hour.' (c) 'A train made 3 stops today.'

steps.math: unit rate = a rate compared to exactly 1
steps.annotation: Start from the definition: two different units, second amount exactly 1.
It's a rate, but 3 is not 1, so it's not a UNIT rate.
'Per hour' means per 1 hour. The hidden 1 makes this the unit rate.
No comparison at all, so it isn't even a rate. Answer: b.

faded_example.stem: Which statement describes a unit rate? (a) '$36 for 4 tickets' (b) '$9 per ticket' (c) 'She bought 4 tickets.'

steps.math: Test each: is the second amount exactly 1?
steps.annotation: That's the only test that matters.

steps.math: (a) $36 : 4 tickets -- 4 is not 1, so not a unit rate
steps.annotation: A rate, but not scaled to 1.
Check (b): what does 'per ticket' really mean? Is there a hidden 1?
Check (c), then state which letter is the unit rate.

skills.name: Determine the unit rate from a given ratio
skills.i_do_script: Now we don't just spot unit rates — we MAKE them. Take the ratio 9 to 3. To find the unit rate, I divide BOTH numbers by the second one: 9 / 3 = 3, and 3 / 3 = 1. The ratio becomes 3 to 1, so the unit rate is 3. A rate table makes this visible: 3 pairs with 1, 6 pairs with 2, 9 pairs with 3 — walk the table down to the column where the bottom number is 1, and the top number is your unit rate.

canonical_error.pattern: Reports the given ratio (or just its first number) as the unit rate instead of dividing both quantities down to a second quantity of 1
canonical_error.example: For the ratio 12 to 4, student answers '12' or '12:4' instead of dividing to get 3 (the ratio 3:1)
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'unit rate' as a label for the ratio itself rather than the result of scaling it. They haven't internalized that finding the unit rate is an ACTION — divide both parts by the second quantity until the second part is 1.

skills.item_template: A ratio given in words, colon, or fraction form (whole numbers, compatible), often with a rate table to complete. Student finds the unit rate — the value paired with 1. Short response or table completion; data_table figure.

sample_items.stem:
A ratio is given: 9 to 3.

Complete the table to show the unit rate for the given ratio.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9 signals reporting the first number of the ratio; 6 signals subtracting 9 - 3; 27 signals multiplying

sample_items.stem:
A ratio is given: 12 to 4.

Complete the table to show the unit rate for the given ratio.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12 signals reporting the ratio's first number; 8 signals subtracting; 48 signals multiplying

sample_items.stem: A ratio is given: 10 to 2. What is the unit rate for the given ratio?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 10 reports the first number; 8 subtracts 10 - 2; 20 multiplies 10 x 2

sample_items.stem: A ratio is given: 24 to 6. What is the unit rate, written as a ratio with a colon?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 24:6 is the unchanged ratio (canonical error); 1:4 flips the division; 18:1 subtracts instead of divides

sample_items.stem:
A ratio is given: 16 to 8.

Complete the table to show the unit rate for the given ratio.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 16 reports the first number; 8 signals subtraction (16 - 8); 4 signals halving the wrong quantity

redirect_script.stop: Wait — a unit rate ends in a 1.
redirect_script.prompt: Look at the second number in your answer. Is it a 1? If not, you're not done: divide BOTH numbers of the ratio by that second number and write the new pair. Keep going until the pair reads 'something to 1.'
redirect_script.praise: You divided both parts down to 1 — that's exactly how a ratio becomes a unit rate.

vocabulary.definition: The value paired with 1 when a ratio is scaled down — the ratio 'something to 1.'
A table of equivalent pairs for a ratio; the unit rate sits in the column where the second quantity is 1.
Divide both parts of a ratio by the same number to get an equivalent, smaller ratio.

worked_example_script.text: Write the ratio '9 to 3' on the board, and draw a two-row table: top row blank, blank, 9; bottom row 1, 2, 3.
The bottom row counts 1, 2, 3. The 9 sits above the 3. What is this table telling us about how the two quantities travel together?
If 9 pairs with 3, what has to pair with 1? What operation gets you there?
Divide both parts by the second number: 9 / 3 = 3 and 3 / 3 = 1. The ratio 9 to 3 is the same comparison as 3 to 1 — and 'something to 1' is the unit rate.
Fill the table: 3 above 1, 6 above 2, 9 above 3. Circle the '3 over 1' column and label it UNIT RATE.
If the student says the unit rate of 12 to 4 is '12' or '12:4,' don't correct — point at the second number and ask, 'Is that a 1 yet?' The unfinished 1 exposes the error.
Check it forward: does the 3-to-1 column really grow back into the 9-to-3 column if you multiply both parts by 3?
Your turn with the table method: the ratio is 20 to 5. Draw the bottom row 1 through 5 and find what sits above the 1.

practice_problems.stem: The ratio 8 to 2 scales down to ___ to 1.
In a rate table, the unit rate is the value paired with which number?
A ratio is given: 15 to 3. Complete the rate table to find the unit rate.
practice_problems.answer: 5 (table top row: 5, 10, 15 over bottom row 1, 2, 3)
practice_problems.notes: Have students say the division out loud: 15 / 3 = 5 and 3 / 3 = 1.

practice_problems.stem: A ratio is given: 18 to 6. What is the unit rate, written with a colon?
practice_problems.notes: Expect 18:6 from students making the canonical error — the ratio isn't scaled yet.

practice_problems.stem: Keisha found a unit rate. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Keisha wrote: 'The unit rate is 20 to 5.'
practice_problems.answer: Keisha never scaled the ratio — the second number must be 1. Divide both parts by 5: 20 / 5 = 4 and 5 / 5 = 1, so the unit rate is 4 (the ratio 4 to 1).
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error with fresh numbers: reporting the given ratio as the unit rate.

practice_problems.stem: A ratio is given: 28 to 4. Find the unit rate, then name the multiplication that grows 'your answer to 1' back into '28 to 4.'
practice_problems.answer: 7; multiply both parts of 7:1 by 4 to get 28:4.
practice_problems.notes: The backward check makes scaling visible in both directions.

practice_problems.stem: A ratio of 7 to 2 doesn't divide evenly. What is its unit rate?
practice_problems.answer: 3.5 (7 / 2 = 3.5, so the ratio is 3.5 to 1)
practice_problems.notes: The spec allows non-whole answers when identifying a unit rate — the divide-by-the-second-number move doesn't change.

practice_problems.stem: Write a ratio of your own whose unit rate is 6, then a DIFFERENT ratio with the same unit rate.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 12 to 2 and 30 to 5 — both scale down to 6 to 1.
practice_problems.notes: Producing two shows the student sees a whole family of ratios behind one unit rate.

activities.title: Ratio Meets Its Unit Rate
materials: 8 ratio cards and 10 unit-rate cards (two decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Match each ratio to its unit rate. Two unit-rate cards are decoys that match nothing.
3. Rule: to claim a match, say the division out loud ('24 divided by 6 is 4, so 24 to 6 is 4 to 1').
4. Debrief: what did the decoys do to try to fool you?

activities.title: Walk the Table to 1
activities.instructions:
1. Give the group a ratio like 15 to 3. They build the '3' column first: 15 counters above the numeral 3.
2. Ask: if 3 of the bottom unit gets 15, what does 1 get? Students deal the 15 counters into 3 equal shares and put one share above the 1.
3. Fill the whole table (5 above 1, 10 above 2, 15 above 3) and circle the column with the 1.
4. Repeat with 12 to 4 and 18 to 2. Debrief: the unit rate always lives above the 1.

activities.title: Fix Keisha's Unit Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Keisha's work silently and write the exact step where it went wrong.
2. They must fix it with a rate table: bottom row 1 through 5, showing what pairs with 1.
3. Share out: what does the answer to 'what is the unit rate?' always have to end in?

skills.name: Determine the unit rate from a double number line
skills.i_do_script: A double number line is two number lines glued together — top line for one quantity, bottom line for the other, with matching tick marks. Watch me read one: the top line goes 0, 6, 12, 18 and the bottom goes 0, 2, 4, 6. Every tick is a pair: 6 with 2, 12 with 4. To get the unit rate I ask, 'how much on TOP when the BOTTOM is 1?' The bottom isn't showing a 1, so I divide one pair: 6 / 2 = 3. The unit rate is 3 to 1 — even though no tick says so.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the first nonzero pair of tick marks off the diagram and reports it as the unit rate without scaling the bottom to 1
canonical_error.example: For a double number line with top 0, 6, 12, 18 and bottom 0, 2, 4, 6, student answers '6:2' instead of 3 (the ratio 3:1)
canonical_error.why: The student treats the diagram's first labeled pair as 'the rate' and stops. They haven't realized the unit rate may live BETWEEN the printed ticks — the question is always 'what pairs with 1?', which can require dividing and can even produce a decimal the model doesn't show.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a double number line: top labeled 'miles' with ticks 0, 6, 12, 18; bottom labeled 'hours' with ticks 0, 2, 4, 6, lined up vertically.

skills.name: Use a unit rate to test which rate statements are true
skills.i_do_script: Once you know a unit rate, you can predict EVERY amount: multiply the unit rate by how many units you have. A pizza place says 1 large pizza feeds 4 people. So 2 pizzas feed 2 x 4 = 8 people, and 5 pizzas feed 5 x 4 = 20. When a problem hands you statements to judge, I don't guess — I compute the true amount for each one and compare. '3 pizzas feed 6 people'? My math says 3 x 4 = 12, not 6. False.

canonical_error.why: The student hasn't connected 'per 1' to repeated groups — each unit brings its OWN copy of the rate, so scaling is multiplication. Under pressure they merge the two numbers with the friendlier operation, addition.

skills.name: Calculate a unit rate from a real-world rate and use it
skills.i_do_script: This is the full round trip. A runner does 6 laps in 42 minutes. Step one, find the unit rate: 42 minutes divided by 6 laps is 7 — it takes 7 minutes per lap. Step two, USE it: how long for 10 laps? 10 x 7 = 70 minutes. Two moves every time — divide down to 1, then multiply up to whatever the question asks. The only decision is which number gets divided by which, and the units in the question tell you: 'minutes per lap' means minutes get divided by laps.

canonical_error.example: For '6 laps in 42 minutes — find minutes per lap,' student computes 6 / 42 = 1/7 instead of 42 / 6 = 7
canonical_error.why: The student pulls numbers in story order rather than reading the unit phrase. 'Minutes per lap' names the division — the unit before 'per' goes on top (gets divided by the other) — and without that anchor the division direction is a coin flip.

Two numbers, two units. Before dividing anything — which unit does the question put BEFORE the word 'per'?
'Minutes per lap' is an instruction: minutes divided by laps. The unit before 'per' is the one that gets divided.
Label the numbers: 42 MINUTES, 6 LAPS. Set up 42 / 6 and solve: 7.
Say the answer as a full rate sentence. 7 WHAT per WHAT? Does '7 minutes per lap' sound right for a runner?
If the student sets up 6 / 42 because 6 came first in the story, don't correct — ask them to compute it (about 0.14) and check it against sense: 'Could one lap really take a seventh of a minute?'
Now USE the rate: at 7 minutes per lap, how long would 10 laps take? Which operation, and why?
Your turn, both steps: a printer makes 96 copies in 8 minutes. Find copies per minute, then predict copies in 15 minutes.

practice_problems.stem: $24 for 4 pounds of cheese. What is the price per pound?
practice_problems.answer: $6 per pound

practice_problems.stem: At 9 miles per hour, how far do you bike in 3 hours?
practice_problems.answer: 27 miles

practice_problems.stem: A person runs 5 laps in 40 minutes. Part A: minutes per lap? Part B: at that rate, how long for 12 laps?
practice_problems.answer: Part A: 8 minutes per lap (40 / 5); Part B: 96 minutes (12 x 8).
practice_problems.notes: The full round trip: divide down to 1, multiply up.

practice_problems.stem: A factory fills 72 bottles in 6 minutes. Find bottles per minute, then bottles in 25 minutes.
practice_problems.answer: 12 bottles per minute (72 / 6); 300 bottles (25 x 12).
practice_problems.notes: Watch the division direction — 'bottles per minute' puts bottles on top.

practice_problems.stem: Lena found a unit rate. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Problem: A cyclist rides 8 miles in 56 minutes. Find the minutes per mile.
practice_problems.answer: Lena divided in story order — miles first — but 'minutes per mile' says minutes get divided by miles: 56 / 8 = 7 minutes per mile. Her answer fails the sense check too: a mile can't take a seventh of a minute.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error with fresh numbers: story-order division instead of unit-phrase division.

practice_problems.stem: Ground beef costs $18 for 3 pounds at Store A and $28 for 4 pounds at Store B. Which store has the cheaper price per pound?
practice_problems.answer: Store A — $6 per pound (18 / 3) vs $7 per pound (28 / 4).
practice_problems.notes: Comparing rates is the payoff of scaling both to 1.

practice_problems.stem: A car travels 15 miles in 20 minutes. Find the rate in miles per MINUTE (careful — it isn't a whole number), then use it to find miles per hour.
practice_problems.answer: 0.75 miles per minute (15 / 20); 45 miles per hour (0.75 x 60).
practice_problems.notes: Non-whole unit rate plus a unit conversion — the divide-then-multiply structure survives both.

practice_problems.stem: Write a rate story whose unit rate is 12, where the story lists the numbers in REVERSE order of the division (the divisor first).
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'In 4 hours the crew painted 48 fence panels — find panels per hour.' The 4 appears first but 48 / 4 = 12.
practice_problems.notes: The spec's 'difficult' twist: quantities presented in reverse order of the expected unit rate.

activities.title: Story, Division, Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Match each rate story to the division that finds its unit rate. Two division cards are decoys — they divide in story order instead of unit order.
2. To claim a match, read the unit phrase aloud and point at which number lands on top.
3. Debrief: what one word in the question tells you the division direction?

pairs.left: 6 laps in 42 minutes -- minutes per lap
96 pages in 8 days -- pages per day
5 hours to mow 40 lawns -- lawns per hour
120 miles on 4 gallons -- miles per gallon

activities.title: Two-Step Rate Relay
materials: Problem strips with a rate and a scaled question
activities.instructions:
1. Partner A does step one only: find the unit rate and write it as a labeled sentence ('13 dollars per 1 hour').
2. Partner B takes over for step two: use A's unit rate to answer the scaled question ('how much for 20 hours?').
3. B must check A's direction before building on it — if A divided the wrong way, B sends it back with the unit phrase underlined.
4. Swap roles each strip. Debrief: which step hides more mistakes, and why?

activities.title: Best Deal Showdown
materials: Deck of price cards ('$32 for 4 pizzas', '$45 for 5 pizzas')
activities.instructions:
1. Flip two price cards for the same item.
2. Both partners race to find each card's price per 1 item, showing the division on the whiteboard.
3. The pair must agree which is the better deal and say the comparison sentence: '___ per 1 beats ___ per 1.'
4. Trap rounds: some cards list the count before the price ('4 hours for $52') — the unit phrase, not the story order, picks the division.
5. Debrief: why does scaling both prices to 1 make the comparison fair?

strategy_links.why: The division-direction decision is invisible — thinking aloud ('minutes per lap, so minutes on top') externalizes it.
The two-move routine (divide to 1, multiply up) is ideal for I Do / We Do / You Do release.
Story-order division produces absurd rates (1/7 minute per lap) — sense-checking flawed work builds the reflex.

questioning_prompts: Which unit comes before 'per' in the question? So which number gets divided?
Say your answer as a full sentence with both units. Does it make sense in the real world?
You found the unit rate — what does the question want you to DO with it now?
Why do we bother scaling to 1 first instead of jumping straight to 13 batches?
If your Part A were wrong, what would happen to Part B? How could you catch that?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides in story order — computes 6 / 42 for 'minutes per lap' because the 6 came first.
misconception_redirects.say: The question says 'minutes per lap.' Underline the unit BEFORE 'per' — that's the one being divided. Say it as a sentence: 'minutes divided by laps.' Now match each number to its unit and set up the division.
misconception_redirects.praise: You let the units choose the division — that's the move that never fails.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds the unit rate correctly in Part A, then ADDS it to the scale factor in Part B (7 + 10 instead of 7 x 10).
misconception_redirects.say: Part A says every lap costs 7 minutes. If you run 10 laps, each one brings its own 7 — is that adding one 7, or ten 7s?
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied the rate by the count — every lap paid its own 7 minutes.

quick_checks.prompt: $36 for 4 movie tickets — price per ticket, in one line.
quick_checks.look_for: $9 via 36 / 4. An answer of 1/9 or 0.11 diagnoses story-order division; 32 diagnoses subtraction.

quick_checks.prompt: You know a pool fills at 15 gallons per minute. How much in 6 minutes — and which operation did you just use?
quick_checks.look_for: 90 gallons, named as multiplication. Hesitation between x and / on the scaling step means the round trip isn't automatic yet.

sentence_starters: The question says ___ per ___, so I divided ___ by ___.
One ___ takes ___, so ___ of them take ___ x ___.

worked_solution.stem: A person runs 6 laps around a track in 42 minutes. Part A: What is the rate in minutes per lap? Part B: At that rate, how long will 10 laps take?
worked_solution.answer: Part A: 7 minutes per lap; Part B: 70 minutes

steps.annotation: The unit before 'per' gets divided. The question, not the story order, picks the direction.
Divide down to 1. Sense check: 7 minutes for a lap is believable; 6/42 of a minute is not.
Use the rate: every lap brings its own 7 minutes, so multiply.
Dividing the answer back by the laps returns the unit rate — the round trip closes.

faded_example.stem: A store sells 5 pounds of apples for $35. Part A: What is the price per pound? Part B: How much would 9 pounds cost?
faded_example.answer: Part A: $7 per pound; Part B: $63

steps.annotation: The unit before 'per' is the one divided.
Divide down to 1.
Part B: each pound costs $7 — compute 9 x 7.
Check: divide your Part B answer by 9. Do you get the unit rate back?

skills.name: Critique and correct flawed unit-rate reasoning
skills.i_do_script: Now you become the teacher. A student wrote: 'A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. Speed = 2 hours / 120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour.' My critique routine has three checks: (1) UNITS — the question wants miles per hour, so miles must be divided by hours; this student flipped it. (2) ARITHMETIC — 2/120 does equal 1/60, so the arithmetic isn't the bug. (3) SENSE — could a car really go 1/60 of a mile in an hour? Never. A full critique names the error, explains it, and shows the fix: 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour.

canonical_error.pattern: Critiques only the arithmetic and declares flipped-rate work 'correct' because the computation checks out
canonical_error.example: Reviewing 'speed = 2 / 120 = 1/60 mph,' student verifies that 2/120 reduces to 1/60 and concludes there is no error
canonical_error.why: The student equates 'checked' with 'recomputed.' They audit the calculation but never audit the SETUP — whether the right quantity was divided by the right one — so an error that lives in the setup passes their inspection untouched.

skills.item_template: A worked solution to a rate problem containing a setup error (usually an inverted division). Student identifies the error, explains why it's wrong, and provides the corrected unit rate. Constructed response with a numeric correction.

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?

Solution: Speed = 2 hours/120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour

Identify and explain the error the student made in solving the problem. Provide the correct solution.
sample_items.answer: The rate is flipped — 'miles per hour' means miles divided by hours, so time belongs in the denominator. Correct: 120 miles / 2 hours = 60 miles per hour.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who only recheck arithmetic will accept 2/120 = 1/60 and miss the inverted setup; some will 'fix' it to 60 without naming the error

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A swimmer completes 96 laps in 12 hours of practice. How many laps does she swim per hour?

Solution: 12 / 96 = 1/8 lap per hour

Identify and explain the error the student made. Provide the correct solution.
sample_items.answer: The division is inverted — 'laps per hour' puts laps on top: 96 / 12 = 8 laps per hour. 1/8 of a lap per hour fails the sense check for a swimmer at practice.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Accepting the work because 12/96 does reduce to 1/8 signals arithmetic-only checking

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A store sells 15 pounds of dog food for $45. What is the price per pound?

Solution: 15 / 45 = 1/3, so the food costs about $0.33 per pound

Identify and explain the error. Provide the correct price per pound.
sample_items.answer: The student divided pounds by dollars. 'Dollars per pound' means 45 / 15 = $3 per pound. The arithmetic 15/45 = 1/3 is right, but it answers a different question (pounds per dollar).
sample_items.distractor_logic: The flipped answer is a true statement about pounds per dollar — students must catch that it answers the wrong question, not that it computes wrong

sample_items.stem:
A student solved the given problem.

Problem: A plane flies 1,500 miles in 3 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?

Solution: 1500 x 3 = 4,500 miles per hour

Identify and explain the error the student made. Provide the correct solution.
sample_items.answer: The student multiplied instead of dividing. Finding a per-hour amount from 3 hours means splitting: 1500 / 3 = 500 miles per hour. 4,500 mph also fails the sense check — the plane would be faster than any jet.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A different setup bug (wrong operation, not inversion) — checks that the critique routine generalizes beyond 'flip it'

redirect_script.stop: You checked the math — now check the setup.
redirect_script.prompt: Run all three checks out loud: UNITS — what does the question put before 'per,' and is that what got divided? ARITHMETIC — does the computation itself work? SENSE — could that answer happen in real life? An error can hide in any of the three.
redirect_script.praise: You caught an error the calculator can't see — that's setup-level thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Examining someone's work to find and explain exactly where it goes wrong.
The plan of the calculation — which numbers, which operation, which order — before any arithmetic happens.
Asking whether an answer could really happen in the situation, like a car going 1/60 of a mile per hour.
Giving the reason your correction is right, not just the new answer.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.RP.2 — constant of proportionality and proportional relationships.

worked_example_script.text: Post the flawed work: 'Problem: A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour? Solution: Speed = 2 hours / 120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour.'
We're grading this like a teacher. Three checks, always in this order: units, arithmetic, sense.
Check one — UNITS. The question asks for miles per hour. In the student's fraction, what got divided by what?
Check two — ARITHMETIC. Is 2/120 really 1/60? So is the arithmetic the problem here, or not?
This is the trap moment: many students see correct arithmetic and declare the work fine. If that happens, push to check three instead of correcting.
Check three — SENSE. A car drives for an hour and covers 1/60 of a mile. Could that be right? What does that tell you about where the error lives?
The error is in the SETUP: the rate is flipped. 'Miles per hour' means miles divided by hours — 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour. A full critique says all three things: what's wrong, why, and the fix.
Your turn to grade: 'A baker frosts 45 cupcakes in 9 minutes. Rate = 9 / 45 = 1/5 cupcake per minute.' Run the three checks and write the full critique.

practice_problems.stem: The question asks for 'pages per minute.' Which quantity goes in the denominator?
practice_problems.answer: minutes

practice_problems.stem: Sense check only: could '2 miles per hour' be a walking speed? Could '1/50 mile per hour' be a car's highway speed?
practice_problems.answer: Yes — 2 mph is a normal walk. No — 1/50 mph is far too slow for a car; a flipped setup is likely.

practice_problems.stem: Grade this work: 'A hose fills 80 gallons in 16 minutes. Rate = 16 / 80 = 1/5 gallon per minute.' Name the error, explain it, and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Inverted setup — 'gallons per minute' means 80 / 16 = 5 gallons per minute. The arithmetic was fine; the division direction was not.
practice_problems.notes: The full three-part critique: name, explain, fix.

practice_problems.stem: Priya CHECKED a classmate's work. Find the mistake in Priya's checking.
shown_work: Classmate's work: 'A bus travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Speed = 3 / 150 = 1/50 mile per hour.'
Priya wrote: 'I checked: 3 divided by 150 really is 1/50. The work is correct.'
practice_problems.answer: Priya only audited the arithmetic. The setup is flipped: 'miles per hour' requires 150 / 3 = 50 miles per hour. Correct arithmetic on a wrong setup is still a wrong answer — and 1/50 mph fails the sense check.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error, one level up: a flawed critique of flawed work.

practice_problems.stem: Grade this work: 'Tickets are $8 each. For 6 tickets: 8 + 6 = $14.' Name the error, explain it, and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Wrong operation — each ticket costs its own $8, so 6 tickets cost 6 x 8 = $48. Addition merged the count with the rate.
practice_problems.notes: Setup errors aren't always inversions — the routine must catch wrong operations too.

practice_problems.stem: Two students found the unit rate for '210 miles on 10 gallons.' Ava: 210 / 10 = 21 miles per gallon. Ben: 10 / 210 = 1/21 gallon per mile. Who answered 'miles per gallon,' and is the other one WRONG or just answering a different question?
practice_problems.answer: Ava answered miles per gallon (21). Ben's number is actually a true rate — gallons per mile — but it does not answer the question asked. Both critiques matter: setup must match the question.
practice_problems.notes: Subtle: the flipped rate is true information aimed at the wrong target.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own flawed solution to 'A runner covers 24 miles in 4 hours — find miles per hour,' hiding the error in the SETUP while keeping the arithmetic perfect. Trade and critique.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'Speed = 4 / 24 = 1/6 mile per hour' — arithmetic is flawless, setup is inverted. The fix: 24 / 4 = 6 miles per hour.
practice_problems.notes: Designing the trap is the deepest form of owning it.

practice_problems.stem: A student claims: 'Any rate problem can be checked just by re-doing the division on a calculator.' Write two or three sentences arguing for or against, using an example.
practice_problems.answer: Against — a calculator re-verifies arithmetic but can't see whether the setup matches the question. Example: 2 / 120 = 1/60 checks out perfectly, yet 'speed = 1/60 mph' is wrong because miles per hour needs 120 / 2.
practice_problems.notes: Names the meta-lesson of the whole skill.

activities.title: Grade the Grader
materials: Printed slip with the bus problem and Priya's check (below)
activities.instructions:
1. Partners read the classmate's work AND Priya's check of it.
2. First pass: run the three checks (units, arithmetic, sense) on the classmate's work and write where the error lives.
3. Second pass: say exactly what Priya's checking routine was missing.
4. Write the full correction with units labeled.
5. Debrief question: why can a solution with perfect arithmetic still be wrong?

content.worked_problem: Classmate: 'A bus travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Speed = 3 / 150 = 1/50 mile per hour.' Priya's check: '3 divided by 150 is 1/50 — correct!'
content.error_step: The classmate inverted the division; Priya audited only the arithmetic and blessed the flipped setup.
content.why: 'Miles per hour' fixes the setup: miles divided by hours, 150 / 3 = 50 mph. Arithmetic checking can never catch a setup error — only the units and sense checks can.

activities.title: Where Does the Error Live?
activities.instructions:
1. Header cards: Setup error, Arithmetic error, No error.
2. The group sorts each worked solution, running the three checks aloud.
3. Rule: a card can't land until someone states the fix (or, for 'No error,' restates why it survives all three checks).
4. Debrief: which pile was hardest to spot, and which check caught it?

cards.text: 60 pages in 5 days: 60 x 5 = 300 pages per day
84 laps in 7 days: 84 / 7 = 14 laps per day
72 beads on 8 strings: 8 / 72 = 1/9 bead per string

activities.title: Sabotage
materials: A list of clean rate problems
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner takes a clean problem ('A kayaker paddles 18 miles in 3 hours — find mph') and secretly writes a WRONG solution, choosing where to hide the bug: setup or arithmetic.
2. Trade papers. The critic must (a) find the error, (b) name which kind it is, (c) fix it — one point for each.
3. Bonus point to the saboteur if the critic mislabels the error's location.
4. Two rounds each. Debrief: which errors were hardest to hide, and which check exposed them?

strategy_links.why: The skill IS worked-example-plus-error-analysis — pairing a correct solution beside the flipped one makes the setup difference visible.
Critiques improve when rehearsed aloud: partners must convince each other where the error lives before writing.
Modeling the three-check routine (units, arithmetic, sense) as a think-aloud gives students a script for auditing setup, not just computation.

questioning_prompts: Where does the error live — the setup or the arithmetic? How do you know?
The question says 'miles per hour.' What did the student actually divide?
Does the answer survive a sense check? Could that number happen in real life?
The student's arithmetic is perfect. Can the answer still be wrong? Why?
Your critique names the error — now what's the fix, with units?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student recomputes the arithmetic, finds it correct, and declares flipped-rate work 'fine.'
misconception_redirects.say: Run all three checks out loud: UNITS — what does the question put before 'per,' and is that what got divided? ARITHMETIC — does the computation itself work? SENSE — could that answer happen in real life? An error can hide in any of the three.
misconception_redirects.praise: You caught an error the calculator can't see — that's setup-level thinking.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student jumps straight to the right answer ('it's 60') without naming or explaining the error.
misconception_redirects.say: Half credit so far — the problem asks you to identify and EXPLAIN the error. Point at the student's fraction and tell me what they divided and what they should have divided.
misconception_redirects.praise: Now that's a full critique: the error, the why, and the fix.

quick_checks.prompt: In one sentence: what's wrong with 'speed = 2 hours / 120 miles'?
quick_checks.look_for: 'The rate is flipped — miles belong on top / time in the denominator.' A student who says 'nothing, 2/120 = 1/60' is auditing arithmetic only.

quick_checks.prompt: Name the three checks in order.
quick_checks.look_for: Units, arithmetic, sense. Missing 'units' predicts they'll keep blessing inverted setups.

sentence_starters: The error is in the ___ because the question asks for ___ per ___.
The arithmetic is ___, but the setup should be ___ divided by ___.

worked_solution.stem: A student solved: 'A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?' Solution: 'Speed = 2 hours / 120 miles = 1/60 miles per hour.' Identify and explain the error, then give the correct solution.
worked_solution.answer: The rate is flipped; correct speed = 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour.

steps.math: check UNITS: 'miles per hour' -> miles / hours
steps.annotation: The question fixes the setup: miles on top, hours in the denominator. The student wrote hours / miles — flipped.
The computation itself has no bug — which is exactly why arithmetic-only checking misses this error.

steps.math: check SENSE: 1/60 mile in an hour?
steps.annotation: A car covering 1/60 of a mile per hour is absurd — confirmation the setup is wrong.

steps.math: fix: 120 miles / 2 hours = 60 miles per hour
steps.annotation: Name it, explain it, fix it: the rate was inverted; time belongs in the denominator; the speed is 60 mph.

faded_example.stem: A student solved: 'A pump moves 180 gallons in 4 minutes. How many gallons per minute?' Solution: '4 / 180 = 1/45 gallon per minute.' Critique and correct.
faded_example.answer: Setup is inverted; correct rate = 180 / 4 = 45 gallons per minute.

steps.annotation: The question demands gallons on top; the student divided minutes by gallons.
No arithmetic bug; the error lives upstream.
SENSE check: could a pump move 1/45 of a gallon each minute? Say why not.
Write the fix: divide the right way and label the units.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5 (find a unit rate in context and use it) -- the At-Proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, move to S6 (critique flawed rate reasoning). If they fail, split the diagnosis: S1 checks whether they even recognize the per-1 idea, and S2 checks whether they can scale a ratio down to 1. S3 (models) and S4 (scaling up) branch off those results.
